text:
do you see type checkers, linters, CI, static analysis, compilers and libraries also as being a meat proxy and not thinking for yourself?


That's an interesting question. The answer very much depends on the kind of tool we're talking about.

I love static type checking. I'm willing to pay the cost of an incomplete type system to have a sound one, though I also appreciate having an (explicit) escape hatch in the rare cases I need it. That stuff catches a ton of the nastiest bugs quickly, efficiently, and reliably. I have no problem shutting my brain down and trust that tool. I'll have to boot it back up anyway as I work on the fix.

I love most compiler warnings, if that's what you mean by linters.

I hate code formatters. Enforcing a set of rules is ok, but the "one-true" clang-format is never satisfactory. Every time a project uses this crap, it takes me less than a day to format the code better than it does, and have the whole team agree with me. Sadly though, it seems many programmers have so little attention to detail they can't format their code correctly without it. (Honestly I'm tempted to fire the lot of them: that lack of attention to detail affects more than code formatting. It damages the code structure, part of its architecture, performance, even user-facing UI and functionality.)

I don't know about static analysis. As long as its behaviour is stable I expect to like them, similar to compiler warnings and linter suggestions.

Libraries, that depends. For quick and dirty projects I'll just trust the most convenient thing I can get my hands on. For serious stuff however I'd minimise my dependencies, seriously evaluate those I do take on, and wrap them around an API of my own design to avoid vendor lock-in.

LLMs... haven't been much help to me to be honest. And I like to code. Even if an LLM could do the job faster and better than I do, I'd still prefer to do it myself. Understanding gives me joy, I don't want to give that up at any level. They're fantastic search engines though. I don't trust them with anything, but they're great at giving me pieces of jargon to get me started. Still, I try to minimise my use, this shit as it stands being so freaking unethical.

Most open source projects are labours of love. They exist because the maintainers like doing it.

Once it starts feeling like work, chances are high that the project gets abandoned or that the maintainer takes a longer break from it.

text:
LLMs do find the occasional bug, it's true, and sometimes that bug probably would not have been noticed by human reviewers. But the LLMs aren't consistent. Sometimes they demand every single constant be represented by a #define (or the equivalent), sometimes they don't. Sometimes they want excruciating null-checks, or thorough array-length checks, sometimes they don't.  They get hung up on code that can't follow "best practices", and is excruciatingly commented as to why and how.

These are but a few examples of many categories they're inconsistent about.

There are social side effects. The fact that The Machine Hath Spoken from On High means that a developer can't effectively argue with them: every other human reviewer has had their opinion framed by the LLM's output. The person using the LLM for review has typically turned their critical evaluation skills off, as well, and isn't going to contribute anything more. LLM-generated reviews are much harder to comprehend than human-written reviews. Sentence structure is convoluted. Vocabulary choice is often fairly exotic. Human limitations and cognitive biases come into play, and the aftereffects aren't pretty.

LLM code reviews seem miraculous the first time they happen, but after a while, experience shows you the problems. They're not worth it on the whole.

text:
Yeah, both were introduced knowingly.

My biggest problem here is the lack of a standard assert that's guaranteed to trigger no matter the compilation options, and is portable on any environment including the smallest micro-controller. The only way would be one the user can customise with #define, but it's cumbersome, and the default probably would have to be no-op for backward compatibility. Possible, but ugly, and not that useful if the default is no-op.

A return code is no good: one would have to remember to check it if they need to, in which case they might as well check their inputs directly. And it's a burden on those who use it correctly by construction, and therefore don't need to check. Plus, early retuning with an error code is worse than UB in many situations. Total loss of security instead of a clean crash in the worst cases.

Some things, like the validity of a pointer or the real size of a buffer, are impossible to check. No matter what I do, it won't be perfect, I need to choose. My choice so far is to simplify the programs of those who do it right, at the expense of those who mess things up. I design the API I want to use. It's also the API that's easiest to write wrappers around. You got a problem with my lack of safety? You can trivially wrap it in. The reverse is not as easy.

The BLAKE2 key init can be made safer, likely at the expense of a tiny bit of performance, by using the update facility and allowing arbitrarily long keys. The official limit though is 64 bytes, and going out of my way to accept more reeks of embrace and extend: it would endorse going out of specs, and lock my users into my library. Which I absolutely do not want: users must be able to switch to faster implementations later on if they want or need to. (HMAC-SHA-512 in the optional file has the exact same conundrum.)

X25519 does reject low order points, in a way: whenever one of the points has low order, the result is all zeroes. Easy to check with crypto_verify32(), and unneeded in practice: most protocols don't need this check to begin with.

About EdDSA, your LLM is dead wrong: accepting low-order points is not an issue. Daniel Bernstein's TweetNaCl accepts them, and so does RFC 8032. The reason it is no issue at all is because you're supposed to vet the public key out of band to begin with. If you don't, an attacker can just provide a key they control, and no structural check (low-order key, non-trivial low-order component, non-canonical encoding) will catch this.

So, for maximum compatibility and optimisation potential, I've gone with the most permissive option possible. I explicitly disagree with libsodium's choice on this issue. Full rationale here. I also highly recommend Henry de Valence's analysis.

crypto_chacha20_ietf returns a u32 counter; past 256 GiB the counter overflows into the nonce word. Documented limit, not a bug, but easy to hit in a file-encryption tool.


Not sure why Claude mentions this: the 256 GiB limit comes from the primitive itself, there's no avoiding it. It's right, though. Correct. Instead of writing x << 26, which is UB/nasal demons when x is negative, we write x * (1<<26), and rely on the compiler to simplify that back to a left shift. So far, the LLM patch reviews I've witnessed tend to produce two kinds of problem reports.

One, trivial things that ought be caught by pre-commit and/or CI, which this particular project does not have for hysterical raisins.  I guess you could say "Praise Strife, the GPUs have freed us from the drudgery of configuring linters", if that benefit outweighs the costs in your personal calculus; even without going into the externalities, I enjoy tooling rabbit holes, so well.

Two, for "vintage" projects, there's just no end to the litany of warts the LLMs will find.  More often than not the maintainers are already well-aware, and I suppose the responsible thing to do, for the sake of human reviewers too, would be sticking a comment like FIXME: should $DTRT here, but see org/team&750, but (1) for organizational issues that cross codebase boundaries, annotating every instance of an idiosyncrasy becomes passive-aggression more than information; though hey, if you've successfully encoded your whole team culture into what the LLM can reach during review (the patch? the tree? all branches? the issue tracker? wikis?) Over & over, for every single wart that's already got you staring at the ceiling at night?

(Someone replied to me re. that last point, "haha, spoken like someone who doesn't have kids; they make you very nag-resilient".  Smiled and moved on, figured it wasn't worth pointing out that in that analogy, the kid is nagging you about things you are convinced are necessary and personally haunt you; lashing out and asking them to imagine their kid pleading for food or medicine would probably not have achieved much)

Can't deny there is the occasional useful and actionable report; I'd smugly counter that the proposed fix is rarely to my taste, focuses on piling local fixups instead of more ambitious architectural cleanups, but then I take a hard look at my backlog of such cleanups, get in that mood again, and have to wonder if the bot knows and is just getting back at us.

I think people need to see the evidence that LLM-coded products are reliable-ish over a long period of time, that they don't continue to cause security incidents at the same rate over time, that the price of LLM-generated code does not start creeping up after wide adoption, etc. Most people will take a decade as a long enough time horizon to judge this on. I don't have a lot of evidence for this, but consider an example: Tesla Roadster came out in 2008 (the first Li-Ion road-legal electric car in the US) and the electric vehicle sales did not start going up consistently YoY till about 2021. By that time, there were enough variants, and reliability data that people were willing to ditch the old normal.

So let's say we have another decade and a bit of human programming as a viable career option for the masses. The current generation of programmers would be towards the middle or end of their careers by then. The new generation of programmers will have come up in the world of LLM-generated code being normal and maybe even the norm. These folks are currently pre-teens. They will have lots of time to adapt to this world. I am OK with this.

I am also okay with LLMs being the way most code is generated. What I am not okay with is that this power (foundational models) living in the hands of few companies. I really hope that LLMs become commoditised and companies like Anthropic and Mistral have to find other ways to make money than renting out their models. Then I can go live out my life hand-building programs as a hobby, just like I did for years before I got paid for it.
